problems.title: Two Sum
problems.summary: Return the indices of the two numbers in nums that add up to target. Exactly one answer exists; don't use an element twice. Any order.
problems.approach: One pass with a hash map from value to index: before storing x, look up target - x. O(n) time.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.summary: Given a string of ()[]{}, return whether every bracket closes in the right order with the right type.
problems.approach: Push openers on a stack; each closer must match the top. Valid if the stack ends empty.

problems.title: Reverse String
problems.summary: Reverse the array of characters s in place with O(1) extra memory. Return nothing.
problems.approach: Two pointers from both ends, swapping until they meet.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.summary: Return whether t is an anagram of s (same letters, same counts).
problems.approach: Compare letter counts (a Counter or a 26-slot array).

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.summary: Buy on one day and sell on a later day. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profit is possible.
problems.approach: Track the lowest price so far; the best profit is max(price - lowest) over one pass.

problems.title: Contains Duplicate
problems.summary: Return true if any value appears at least twice in nums.
problems.approach: A set drops duplicates; compare sizes. O(n).

problems.title: Invert Binary Tree
problems.summary: Mirror the binary tree (swap every node's left and right children) and return its root. Yes, that one, the whiteboard problem that launched a thousand tweets.
problems.approach: Recursively invert both subtrees and swap them. Every node is visited once.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List
problems.summary: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.
problems.approach: Walk the list once, pointing each node's next at the previous node.

problems.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problems.summary: Return the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path.
problems.approach: Depth = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)); an empty tree has depth 0.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.summary: Splice two sorted linked lists into one sorted list and return its head.
problems.approach: Use a dummy head; repeatedly attach the smaller front node, then append the leftover list.

problems.title: Climbing Stairs
problems.summary: You climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways reach step n?
problems.approach: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2): it's Fibonacci. Iterate with two variables.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.summary: Ignoring case and every non-alphanumeric character, does s read the same both ways?
problems.approach: Filter to lowercase alphanumerics, then compare with the reverse (or use two pointers).

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
Was it a car or a cat I saw?

problems.title: Fizz Buzz
problems.summary: Return strings for 1..n: "FizzBuzz" for multiples of 15, "Fizz" for 3, "Buzz" for 5, else the number.
problems.approach: Check 15 first, then 3, then 5. The interview is about not panicking.

problems.title: Majority Element
problems.summary: Return the element that appears more than n/2 times (it always exists).
problems.approach: Boyer-Moore voting: keep a candidate and a counter; the majority survives the cancellations. O(1) space.

problems.title: Move Zeroes
problems.summary: Move all zeros to the end in place, keeping the order of the non-zero elements. Return nothing.
problems.approach: A write pointer marks the next slot for a non-zero; swap each non-zero into it.

problems.title: Binary Search
problems.summary: Return the index of target in sorted, distinct nums, or -1. Must be O(log n).
problems.approach: Halve the search range each step by comparing with the middle element.

problems.title: Roman to Integer
problems.summary: Convert a Roman numeral (1 to 3999) to an integer. A smaller symbol before a larger one is subtracted (IV = 4).
problems.approach: Add each symbol's value, but subtract it when the next symbol is larger.

problems.title: Single Number
problems.summary: Every element appears twice except one. Find it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
problems.approach: XOR everything: pairs cancel to 0, leaving the single number.

problems.title: Missing Number
problems.summary: nums holds n distinct numbers from 0..n. Return the one that's missing.
problems.approach: Expected sum 0..n minus the actual sum (or XOR indices with values).

problems.title: Longest Common Prefix
problems.summary: Return the longest prefix shared by every string in strs (empty string if none).
problems.approach: The common prefix of all strings equals that of the lexicographic min and max.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.summary: Group the strings that are anagrams of each other. Any order, both for the groups and inside them.
problems.approach: Key each word by its sorted letters (or a 26-count tuple) and bucket by key.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.summary: Return the length of the longest substring of s with no repeated characters.
problems.approach: Sliding window: remember each char's last index and jump the window start past a repeat.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.summary: Return the k most frequent elements (the answer is unique). Any order.
problems.approach: Count, then bucket by frequency and read buckets from high to low. O(n); a heap gives O(n log k).

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.summary: Return answer[i] = product of all elements except nums[i], in O(n) and without division.
problems.approach: Prefix products left-to-right into the output, then multiply by suffix products right-to-left.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.summary: Return every unique triplet that sums to 0. No duplicate triplets; any order.
problems.approach: Sort, fix each first element, then two-pointer the rest; skip equal values to avoid duplicates. O(n²).

problems.title: Container With Most Water
problems.summary: Pick two lines that, with the x-axis, hold the most water. Return that area.
problems.approach: Two pointers from the ends; always move the shorter line inward, because it caps the area.

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.summary: Count the islands of '1' cells (connected up/down/left/right) in a grid of '1'/'0'.
problems.approach: Scan the grid; each unvisited '1' starts a new island, and a DFS/BFS sinks its whole component.

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.summary: Return the fewest coins (unlimited supply of each) that sum to amount, or -1 if impossible.
problems.approach: Bottom-up DP: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - coin]). Greedy fails (try coins [1,3,4], amount 6).

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.summary: Return the longest palindromic substring of s. (These tests all have a single longest answer.)
problems.approach: Expand around each of the 2n-1 centers (characters and gaps). O(n²) time, O(1) space.

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.summary: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated. Return the index of target or -1, in O(log n).
problems.approach: Binary search; one half around mid is always sorted, so check if target lies inside it.

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.summary: Merge all overlapping intervals (touching counts as overlapping) and return the result.
problems.approach: Sort by start; extend the last merged interval while the next one starts before it ends.

problems.title: Rotate Image
problems.summary: Rotate an n×n matrix 90° clockwise in place. Return nothing.
problems.approach: Transpose, then reverse each row.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problems.summary: Return the k-th largest element (in sorted order, not the k-th distinct).
problems.approach: Keep a min-heap of size k; its top is the answer. O(n log k). Quickselect averages O(n).

problems.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problems.summary: Is this a valid BST? Every left-subtree value is strictly less than the node, every right-subtree value strictly greater.
problems.approach: Pass down (low, high) bounds; checking only the direct children misses deeper violations.

problems.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problems.summary: Return node values level by level, left to right.
problems.approach: BFS one level at a time.

problems.title: Daily Temperatures
problems.summary: For each day, how many days until a warmer temperature? 0 if never.
problems.approach: Monotonic decreasing stack of indices; a warmer day resolves every colder day on the stack.

problems.title: House Robber
problems.summary: Rob houses for maximum money without robbing two adjacent houses.
problems.approach: DP with two states: best if you rob this house vs. skip it.

problems.title: Subsets
problems.summary: Return every subset of distinct nums (the power set). Any order.
problems.approach: Start with [[]]; for each number, add it to a copy of every subset so far. 2ⁿ results.

problems.title: Word Break
problems.summary: Can s be split into a sequence of dictionary words (reuse allowed)?
problems.approach: DP: ok[i] is true if some ok[j] holds and s[j:i] is a word.

problems.title: Spiral Matrix
problems.summary: Return all elements of an m×n matrix in clockwise spiral order.
problems.approach: Peel the top row, rotate the rest counter-clockwise, repeat (or walk four shrinking boundaries).

problems.title: Jump Game
problems.summary: From index 0, each value is your max jump length. Can you reach the last index?
problems.approach: Greedy: track the farthest reachable index; fail if you ever stand beyond it.

problems.title: Decode Ways
problems.summary: Digits map to letters (1 = A … 26 = Z). Count the ways to decode the digit string s.
problems.approach: Fibonacci-like DP: a valid single digit carries ways[i-1], a valid two-digit 10..26 adds ways[i-2].

problems.title: Edit Distance
problems.summary: Minimum inserts, deletes, and replacements to turn word1 into word2.
problems.approach: Levenshtein DP over prefixes: match is free, else 1 + min(replace, delete, insert).

problems.title: Unique Paths
problems.summary: A robot moves only right or down on an m×n grid. How many paths go from top-left to bottom-right?
problems.approach: Choose which m-1 of the m+n-2 moves go down: C(m+n-2, m-1). Or DP row by row.

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problems.summary: Length of the longest run of consecutive integers in unsorted nums, in O(n).
problems.approach: Put everything in a set; only start counting from numbers with no predecessor.

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
problems.summary: Given bar heights, how much rain water is trapped between the bars?
problems.approach: Two pointers: the shorter side's running max bounds its water. O(n) time, O(1) space.

problems.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.summary: Return the median of the two sorted arrays combined, in O(log(m+n)).
problems.approach: Binary-search a partition of the shorter array so the left halves hold the smaller (m+n+1)/2 values.

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.summary: Return the shortest substring of s containing every character of t (with multiplicity), or "".
problems.approach: Sliding window with a need-counter: grow until all chars are covered, then shrink from the left.

problems.title: Sliding Window Maximum
problems.summary: Return the maximum of each window of size k as it slides left to right.
problems.approach: Monotonic deque of indices with decreasing values; the front is the window max. O(n).

problems.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
problems.summary: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
problems.approach: Min-heap of the k list heads (tie-break by index); pop the smallest, push its successor. O(N log k).

problems.title: First Missing Positive
problems.summary: Return the smallest positive integer missing from nums, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
problems.approach: Cyclic sort: put each value v in 1..n at index v-1; the first index i with nums[i] != i+1 is the answer.

problems.title: N-Queens
problems.summary: Return every placement of n non-attacking queens on an n×n board, each as rows of 'Q'/'.'. Boards in any order.
problems.approach: Backtrack row by row, tracking used columns and both diagonals (r-c and r+c).

problems.title: Regular Expression Matching
problems.summary: Does pattern p match all of s? . matches any char; x* matches zero or more of x.
problems.approach: Memoized recursion on (i, j): with a '*' next, either skip 'x*' or consume one matching char.

problems.title: Wildcard Matching
problems.summary: Does pattern p match all of s? ? matches one char; * matches any sequence, including empty.
problems.approach: Greedy with backtracking to the last '*': on a mismatch, let that star absorb one more character.

problems.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
problems.summary: A path follows parent/child edges, can start and end anywhere, and has at least one node. Return the max path sum.
problems.approach: Post-order: each node returns its best downward gain (negative gains clipped to 0); the answer bends at some node.

problems.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
problems.summary: Return the area of the largest rectangle that fits under the histogram (bar width 1).
problems.approach: Monotonic increasing stack of (start, height); popping a bar finalizes the widest rectangle at its height.

problems.title: Longest Valid Parentheses
problems.summary: Return the length of the longest well-formed parentheses substring of s.
problems.approach: A stack of indices seeded with -1; after each ')' the top marks where the current valid run began.

problems.title: Word Ladder
problems.summary: Change one letter at a time, each step a word in wordList. Return the number of words in the shortest sequence from beginWord to endWord, or 0.
problems.approach: BFS over words; neighbors differ by one letter (try all 26 letters per position).

problems.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
problems.summary: For each nums[i], count how many elements to its right are smaller.
problems.approach: Scan right-to-left with a Fenwick tree over value ranks: query the count of smaller ranks, then add. O(n log n).

problems.title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
problems.summary: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing path, moving up/down/left/right.
problems.approach: DFS with memoization: the longest path from a cell is 1 + the best increasing neighbor. Strictness makes it a DAG.

problems.title: Combine Two Tables
problems.summary: Report the firstName, lastName, city, state of every person in Person. If a person has no row in Address, report null for city and state. Any order.
problems.approach: LEFT JOIN Address onto Person so people without an address still appear, with NULLs.

solution.sql: SELECT p.firstName, p.lastName, a.city, a.state FROM Person p LEFT JOIN Address a ON a.personId = p.personId

schema: CREATE TABLE Person (personId INT, lastName VARCHAR(255), firstName VARCHAR(255))
CREATE TABLE Address (addressId INT, personId INT, city VARCHAR(255), state VARCHAR(255))

problems.title: Employees Earning More Than Their Managers
problems.summary: Find every employee whose salary is strictly greater than the salary of their manager (the row whose id equals their managerId). Return one column, Employee, with their names. Any order.
problems.approach: Self-join Employee to itself on managerId = id, then keep rows where the employee out-earns the manager.

solution.sql: SELECT e.name AS Employee FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON m.id = e.managerId WHERE e.salary > m.salary

schema: CREATE TABLE Employee (id INT, name VARCHAR(255), salary INT, managerId INT)

problems.title: Duplicate Emails
problems.summary: Report every email that appears in more than one row of Person, once each, in a column named Email. Any order.
problems.approach: GROUP BY email and keep the groups with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.

solution.sql: SELECT email AS Email FROM Person GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

schema: CREATE TABLE Person (id INT, email VARCHAR(255))

problems.title: Customers Who Never Order
problems.summary: List the names of customers who have no row in Orders, in a column named Customers. Any order.
problems.approach: Anti-join: keep customers for whom NOT EXISTS an order with their id (or LEFT JOIN and test for NULL).

solution.sql: SELECT c.name AS Customers FROM Customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.customerId = c.id)

schema: CREATE TABLE Customers (id INT, name VARCHAR(255))
CREATE TABLE Orders (id INT, customerId INT)

problems.title: Big Countries
problems.summary: A country is big if its area is at least 3,000,000 km² or its population is at least 25,000,000. Return name, population, area of the big countries. Any order.
problems.approach: A plain WHERE with OR; note both thresholds are inclusive (>=).

solution.sql: SELECT name, population, area FROM World WHERE area >= 3000000 OR population >= 25000000

schema: CREATE TABLE World (name VARCHAR(255), continent VARCHAR(255), area INT, population INT, gdp BIGINT)

problems.title: Find Customer Referee
problems.summary: Return the name of every customer who was not referred by the customer with id = 2. Customers with no referee (NULL) count. Any order.
problems.approach: referee_id <> 2 is UNKNOWN for NULL rows, so add an explicit OR referee_id IS NULL.

solution.sql: SELECT name FROM Customer WHERE referee_id IS NULL OR referee_id <> 2

schema: CREATE TABLE Customer (id INT, name VARCHAR(25), referee_id INT)

problems.title: Rising Temperature
problems.summary: Return the id of every day whose temperature is higher than the temperature on the previous calendar day. Days without a record for the day before do not count. Any order.
problems.approach: Self-join each day to the row one calendar day earlier (DATEDIFF = 1), not to id - 1, then compare.

solution.sql: SELECT w.id FROM Weather w JOIN Weather y ON DATEDIFF(w.recordDate, y.recordDate) = 1 WHERE w.temperature > y.temperature

schema: CREATE TABLE Weather (id INT, recordDate DATE, temperature INT)

problems.title: Not Boring Movies
problems.summary: Return all columns of the movies with an odd id whose description is not 'boring', ordered by rating descending.
problems.approach: Filter with id % 2 = 1 and description <> 'boring', then ORDER BY rating DESC.

solution.sql: SELECT id, movie, description, rating FROM Cinema WHERE id % 2 = 1 AND description <> 'boring' ORDER BY rating DESC

schema: CREATE TABLE Cinema (id INT, movie VARCHAR(255), description VARCHAR(255), rating FLOAT(2, 1))

problems.title: Article Views I
problems.summary: Find the authors who viewed at least one of their own articles (author_id = viewer_id). Return each one once, in a column named id, sorted ascending.
problems.approach: Keep rows where author_id = viewer_id, SELECT DISTINCT the author, ORDER BY id.

solution.sql: SELECT DISTINCT author_id AS id FROM Views WHERE author_id = viewer_id ORDER BY id

schema: CREATE TABLE Views (article_id INT, author_id INT, viewer_id INT, view_date DATE)

problems.title: Second Highest Salary
problems.summary: Return the second highest distinct salary as a single row with one column, SecondHighestSalary. If there is no second highest salary, return one row containing null.
problems.approach: Wrap DISTINCT ... ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 in a scalar subquery; an empty subquery becomes NULL, so you always get exactly one row.

solution.sql: SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM Employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1) AS SecondHighestSalary

schema: CREATE TABLE Employee (id INT, salary INT)

problems.title: Rank Scores
problems.summary: Rank the scores from highest to lowest. Equal scores share a rank, and the next rank is the next consecutive integer (no gaps). Return score and rank, ordered by score descending.
problems.approach: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) gives gap-free ranks; quote the alias because rank is a function name.

solution.sql: SELECT score, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS "rank" FROM Scores ORDER BY score DESC

schema: CREATE TABLE Scores (id INT, score DECIMAL(3, 2))

problems.title: Consecutive Numbers
problems.summary: id is an autoincrement column. Find every num that appears at least three times in a row (three consecutive ids). Return each one once, in a column named ConsecutiveNums. Any order.
problems.approach: Join Logs to itself at id + 1 and id + 2 with the same num (or compare LAG/LEAD), then DISTINCT.

solution.sql: SELECT DISTINCT l1.num AS ConsecutiveNums FROM Logs l1 JOIN Logs l2 ON l2.id = l1.id + 1 AND l2.num = l1.num JOIN Logs l3 ON l3.id = l1.id + 2 AND l3.num = l1.num

schema: CREATE TABLE Logs (id INT, num INT)

problems.title: Department Highest Salary
problems.summary: For each department, find the employees who have the highest salary in it (ties all count). Return Department, Employee, Salary. Any order.
problems.approach: Compare each salary to its own department's MAX (correlated subquery, or match on (departmentId, MAX(salary)) pairs), then join Department for the name.

solution.sql: SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary FROM Employee e JOIN Department d ON d.id = e.departmentId WHERE e.salary = (SELECT MAX(x.salary) FROM Employee x WHERE x.departmentId = e.departmentId)

schema: CREATE TABLE Employee (id INT, name VARCHAR(255), salary INT, departmentId INT)
CREATE TABLE Department (id INT, name VARCHAR(255))

problems.title: Managers with at Least 5 Direct Reports
problems.summary: Return the name of every manager who has at least five direct reports (rows whose managerId is the manager's id). Any order.
problems.approach: Join managers to their reports, GROUP BY the manager's id (not name), and keep COUNT(*) >= 5.

solution.sql: SELECT m.name FROM Employee m JOIN Employee r ON r.managerId = m.id GROUP BY m.id, m.name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5

schema: CREATE TABLE Employee (id INT, name VARCHAR(255), department VARCHAR(255), managerId INT)

problems.title: Exchange Seats
problems.summary: Swap the seat id of every two consecutive students (1↔2, 3↔4, ...). If the count is odd, the last student keeps their seat. Return id, student ordered by id ascending.
problems.approach: Rewrite the id instead of moving names: even ids go to id - 1, odd ids to id + 1 unless it is the last (MAX) id. Then sort by the new id.

solution.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN id % 2 = 0 THEN id - 1 WHEN id = (SELECT MAX(id) FROM Seat) THEN id ELSE id + 1 END AS id, student FROM Seat ORDER BY 1

schema: CREATE TABLE Seat (id INT, student VARCHAR(255))

problems.title: Game Play Analysis IV
problems.summary:
Report the fraction of players who logged in again on the day right after their first login, rounded to 2 decimal places, as a single column fraction.

Grader note: this runs on SQLite, where integer / integer truncates (5 / 3 = 1). Multiply by 1.0 before you divide.
problems.approach: Find each player's MIN(event_date), LEFT JOIN to a login exactly one day later, and divide the matches by the number of players.

solution.sql: SELECT ROUND(COUNT(a.player_id) * 1.0 / COUNT(*), 2) AS fraction FROM (SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_day FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id) f LEFT JOIN Activity a ON a.player_id = f.player_id AND DATEDIFF(a.event_date, f.first_day) = 1

schema: CREATE TABLE Activity (player_id INT, device_id INT, event_date DATE, games_played INT)

problems.title: Capital Gain/Loss
problems.summary: Every 'Buy' of a stock is later matched by a 'Sell'. Report each stock's total capital gain or loss (sell prices minus buy prices) as stock_name, capital_gain. Any order.
problems.approach: Pairing buys and sells is unnecessary: SUM(price) with buys negated, GROUP BY stock_name.

solution.sql: SELECT stock_name, SUM(CASE WHEN operation = 'Sell' THEN price ELSE -price END) AS capital_gain FROM Stocks GROUP BY stock_name

schema: CREATE TABLE Stocks (stock_name VARCHAR(15), operation VARCHAR(4), operation_day INT, price INT)

problems.title: Department Top Three Salaries
problems.summary: A high earner is an employee whose salary is among the top three distinct salaries of their department. Return Department, Employee, Salary for all high earners. Any order.
problems.approach: DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) and keep rank <= 3; or count the distinct higher salaries in the same department and keep counts < 3.

solution.sql: SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary FROM (SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk FROM Employee) e JOIN Department d ON d.id = e.departmentId WHERE e.rk <= 3

schema: CREATE TABLE Employee (id INT, name VARCHAR(255), salary INT, departmentId INT)
CREATE TABLE Department (id INT, name VARCHAR(255))

problems.title: Trips and Users
problems.summary:
For each day from 2013-10-01 to 2013-10-03, compute the cancellation rate: cancelled requests (by client or driver) divided by all requests, counting only trips whose client and driver are both unbanned. Round to 2 decimals. Return Day and Cancellation Rate; skip days with no such trips. Any order.

Grader note: this runs on SQLite, where integer / integer truncates (5 / 3 = 1). Multiply by 1.0 before you divide.
problems.approach: Join Users twice (client and driver) with banned = 'No', filter the date range, GROUP BY day, and average a 1/0 cancelled flag.

solution.sql: SELECT t.request_at AS Day, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN t.status = 'completed' THEN 0.0 ELSE 1.0 END), 2) AS "Cancellation Rate" FROM Trips t JOIN Users c ON c.users_id = t.client_id AND c.banned = 'No' JOIN Users d ON d.users_id = t.driver_id AND d.banned = 'No' WHERE t.request_at BETWEEN '2013-10-01' AND '2013-10-03' GROUP BY t.request_at

schema: CREATE TABLE Trips (id INT, client_id INT, driver_id INT, city_id INT, status VARCHAR(32), request_at VARCHAR(50))
CREATE TABLE Users (users_id INT, banned VARCHAR(50), role VARCHAR(16))

problems.title: Human Traffic of Stadium
problems.summary: Return every row that belongs to a run of three or more consecutive ids in which each row has people >= 100. Return id, visit_date, people ordered by visit_date ascending.
problems.approach: Gaps and islands: among rows with people >= 100, id - ROW_NUMBER() is constant within each run of consecutive ids. Keep the groups of size >= 3.

solution.sql: WITH good AS (SELECT id, visit_date, people, id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp FROM Stadium WHERE people >= 100), sized AS (SELECT *, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY grp) AS n FROM good) SELECT id, visit_date, people FROM sized WHERE n >= 3 ORDER BY visit_date

schema: CREATE TABLE Stadium (id INT, visit_date DATE, people INT)

quiz.q: What is the average-case time complexity of looking up a key in a hash map?
choices: Depends on how much coffee the hash function had
quiz.why: Hashing goes straight to a bucket; collisions make the worst case O(n), but the average is O(1).

quiz.q: Which command undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged?
quiz.why: --soft moves HEAD back and leaves the index and working tree alone.

quiz.q: In most languages, what does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluate to?
quiz.why: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare floats with a tolerance, or use a decimal type for money.

quiz.q: What is the amortized time complexity of appending to a dynamic array (Python list, Go slice, Rust Vec)?
quiz.why: When the array is full it grows by a constant factor, so the rare O(n) copy averages out to O(1) per append.

quiz.q: Binary search only works if the input has one property. What is it?
quiz.why: Each step discards half the range based on a comparison, which is only valid when the data is sorted (or the predicate is monotonic).

quiz.q: A bad commit is already on the shared main branch. What is the safe way to undo it?
choices: git reset --hard HEAD~1, then git push --force
quiz.why: revert adds a new commit that inverts the bad one, so it does not rewrite history that teammates have already pulled.

quiz.q: Which git command binary-searches the commit history to find the commit that introduced a bug?
quiz.why: You mark one good and one bad commit, and git checks out the midpoint each step. git bisect run <script> automates it.

quiz.q: Which HTTP method is NOT idempotent by definition?
quiz.why: Two identical POSTs can create two resources. Repeated PUT or DELETE calls leave the server in the same state as one call.

quiz.q: The user is logged in, but their role does not allow this action. Which status code fits?
quiz.why: 401 means the server does not know who you are (missing or bad credentials). 403 means it knows who you are, and the answer is still no.

quiz.q: Which HTTP status code tells a client it is being rate limited?
quiz.why: A 429 response often includes a Retry-After header that tells the client how long to wait.

quiz.q: Who enforces CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)?
choices: The intern who last touched the nginx config
quiz.why: The server only sends Access-Control-* headers. The browser decides whether page JavaScript may read the response, which is why curl ignores CORS completely.

quiz.q: What do you call a test that passes and fails on the same code with no changes?
quiz.why: Usual causes: timing and sleeps, shared state between tests, test order, and real network or clock calls.

quiz.q: In the test pyramid, which kind of test should you have the most of?
quiz.why: Unit tests are fast, cheap and point straight at the failure. Slow, brittle end-to-end tests belong at the narrow top.

quiz.q: Your test suite reports 100% line coverage. What does that prove?
choices: Every line ran at least once during the tests
Every combination of branches was tested
You may now skip code review
quiz.why: Coverage measures what executed, not what was checked. A test with no assertions still adds coverage.

quiz.q: A payment request times out and the client retries it. What prevents a double charge?
choices: A unique idempotency key that the server deduplicates on
A strongly worded comment above the retry loop
quiz.why: A timeout does not tell the client whether the first request succeeded. The server stores the result per key and returns it for the retry instead of charging again.

quiz.q: A downstream service is overloaded. How should thousands of clients retry their failed calls?
choices: Exactly once per second, all of them
Open a ticket and retry next quarter
quiz.why: Backoff reduces load while the failure continues, and jitter stops clients from retrying in synchronized waves (a thundering herd).

quiz.q: An ORM loads 100 posts in one query, then runs one more query per post to load its author. What is this anti-pattern called?
quiz.why: Load the authors in one batched query or a JOIN (eager loading) instead of one query per row.

quiz.q: In standard SQL, what does SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at = NULL return?
choices: All rows where deleted_at is NULL
quiz.why: Any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, never TRUE, so no row matches. Use IS NULL.

quiz.q: A table has one index on (last_name, first_name). Which filter can use that index efficiently?
quiz.why: A composite B-tree index is sorted by its leftmost column first, so the filter must start there. Wrapping the column in a function also blocks a normal index lookup.

quiz.q: What is the lowest standard SQL isolation level that prevents dirty reads?
quiz.why: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads. READ COMMITTED only shows committed data, and it is PostgreSQL's default.

quiz.q: def add(item, bucket=[]): bucket.append(item); return bucket. You call add(1), then add(2). What does the second call return?
quiz.why: Python evaluates default values once, when the def runs, so every call shares one list. Use bucket=None and create the list inside the function.

quiz.q: What does [f() for f in [lambda: i for i in range(3)]] return?
choices: A sincere apology from the interpreter
quiz.why: A closure looks up i when it runs, not when it was created, and by then the loop has finished at 2. Bind it early with lambda i=i: i.

quiz.q: In JavaScript, what do 0 == '' and 0 === '' evaluate to?
quiz.why: == coerces both sides first ('' becomes 0). === compares type and value with no coercion, so prefer it.

quiz.q: What does [10, 9, 1].sort() return in JavaScript?
choices: A Promise that resolves to a sorted array, eventually
quiz.why: With no comparator, sort converts the elements to strings and compares them as text. Pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.

quiz.q: What does a TypeScript type annotation or 'as' assertion do at runtime?
choices: It throws if the value has the wrong type
It converts the value to that type
It files a bug report against the backend team
quiz.why: TypeScript checks types only at compile time. Validate untrusted data, such as API responses, at runtime (for example with a schema validator).

quiz.q: Which TypeScript type accepts any value but makes you narrow it before you can use it?
quiz.why: any turns type checking off. unknown keeps it on and makes you check with typeof, instanceof or a type guard first.

quiz.q: In Go, what happens when you assign m["a"] = 1 after var m map[string]int?
choices: It works; Go creates the map lazily
It panics: assignment to entry in nil map
The gopher writes it down for you
quiz.why: A nil map can be read (it returns zero values) but not written. Create it first with make(map[string]int) or a map literal.

quiz.q: *MyErr implements error. func f() error { var p *MyErr; return p }. Is f() != nil true?
choices: Yes, the interface holds a typed nil pointer
Only if go vet is in a bad mood
quiz.why: An interface value is nil only if both its type and its value are nil. Here the type is *MyErr, so the error is not nil. Return a literal nil instead.

quiz.q: In Rust, can a &mut reference and a & reference to the same value both be in use at the same time?
choices: No: many shared references or one mutable reference, never both
Yes, if you ask the borrow checker nicely
quiz.why: The borrow checker enforces aliasing XOR mutation at compile time. That rules out data races and iterator invalidation.

quiz.q: In a Rust function that returns Result, which operator returns the error early if a call fails?
quiz.why: let x = parse(s)?; unwraps an Ok, or converts the Err with From and returns it from the function.

quiz.q: In Ruby, which values are falsy?
choices: Anything written before the first coffee
quiz.why: In Ruby, 0, "" and [] are all truthy. Only false and nil are falsy.

quiz.q: Which Ruby operator calls a method only when the receiver is not nil, and returns nil otherwise?
quiz.why: user&.name returns nil when user is nil, instead of raising NoMethodError.

quiz.q: Why should a C# method avoid async void, except for event handlers?
choices: Callers cannot await it or catch its exceptions
It is slower than async Task
void is bad luck in async code
quiz.why: An exception in an async void method goes to the SynchronizationContext and can crash the process. Return Task instead.

quiz.q: You build one large string from 10,000 pieces in a C# loop. What should you use?
choices: A new thread for each piece
quiz.why: C# strings are immutable, so each += copies the whole string (O(n^2) in total). StringBuilder appends into a growing buffer.
